Increasing cognitive load during few-shot learning will amplify the self-consistency and inter-individual idiosyncrasy of constructed global rankings while enhancing frontoparietal neural representations of the subjective schema at the expense of ground-truth pairwise evidence.

Causal disruption of the frontoparietal cortex via transcranial magnetic stimulation during few-shot pair learning will prevent the construction of self-consistent idiosyncratic global rankings and abolish the post-learning neural representational reorganization that aligns item similarity with subjective rank order.

The specific idiosyncratic global ranking that an individual constructs from identical few-shot pairwise input can be predicted from the intrinsic representational geometry of their frontoparietal cortex measured before any learning occurs.

Following the construction of an idiosyncratic global ranking from few-shot local pairs, individuals will systematically distort memory for newly encountered contradictory pair evidence to conform to their subjective schema, with the degree of distortion predicted by the strength of frontoparietal neural coding for their idiosyncratic ranking.

Pre-learning frontoparietal neural dissimilarity between items predicts the specific idiosyncratic global ranking an individual will construct during few-shot transitive inference, with greater intrinsic representational distance biasing items toward more distant subjective ranks.

Experimentally priming participants with a specific ordinal item feature before few-shot learning predictably biases the direction of their idiosyncratic global ranking distortions, such that individuals receiving the same prime converge on a shared distorted ranking that deviates from ground truth in a feature-consistent direction.
